reviews.title: Pointless and No Features - Why Pay for this at all
reviews.text:
Even when you haven't used the app at all that day and it says in the stats that you have not even opened that app today, it still blocks you out of it. You can't actually tap the home icon from your screen, and it says you have hit your time limit. I understand these apps aim to create barriers to losing time within applications, but it's clear that they have the belief that you can only lose time doom scrolling on social media. That is completely not a reality today.

Me wanting an app that simply introduces an intervention when I'm in a long session doesn't mean that, from the moment I wake up in the morning, the solution is to prevent me from accessing the app and now needing to dig around my phone to find it when it does have a legitimate utility in my life. Yet, at the same time, that app can lose me in long sessions. Two things can be true at once. You can have an app that is essential to your daily life and has a legitimate utility for you, WHILE ALSO being an app that can lead you to lose tremendous time within it. Therefore, you need to catch yourself when you're in long sessions where logically, once you hit a certain interval of time, at that point, it is no longer serving a productive utility but instead stealing your time. 

It's extremely frustrating because apps like this, OneSec, ScreenZen, and seemingly all others that are advertising themselves as specifically effective for intervening doom scrolling are, in reality, not actually effective at all unless you solely want to use it for social media. Outside of that, they are completely archaic to the everyday reality of life.

reviews.title: Almost Perfect
reviews.text:
Absolutely love this app! Definitely helps me limit my scrolling time. The push-up challenge helps keep me in great shape, so it’s almost like having a bonus gym membership, as well—definitely more than worth the price tag.

That being said, there are a few updates that would make it perfect:

(1) if you need to use your app but don’t have any exercise minutes banked, you have to exit any challenge you’re currently participating in. I’ve had times where I need to use an app just for a minute or two (example to find party invite information on a social media account), but I’m out in public and can’t do push-ups. It’s demoralizing to have to leave a challenge. It would be nice to have a minute allotment set aside each day for that type of emergency use.

(2) If you start a challenge for a period of several days, you can’t switch between easy, medium, and hard modes without leaving and losing all your minutes. It’s problematic because depending on how many push-ups I’ve done the day before, my muscles may be fatigued and unable to sustain the same level of activity. At one point I actually developed an overuse injury—I was down for a little over a month, and my screen time sky-rocketed as a result!I manage the problem by sticking to one day challenges, but it would be nice to have the option to enter a longer length challenge and toggle between difficulties depending on how your muscles feel that day.

A near perfect app! Will happily bump to five stars with a few updates.

reviews.text:
Like most Screen Time apps, it relies on three mechanisms:
app time limits unlocks / temporary access
scheduled blocks
The problem is that following or breaking these rules isn't meaningfully tracked. Users can:
• repeatedly use unlocks
• change limits or schedules after
enforcement starts
• revoke Screen Time permissions and
re-enable later(This is due to apple’s screen time API) Apple’s screentime API fundamentally ruins the premise of these screentime apps. 
...without any persistent history or consequence inside the app. That makes it easy to undermine your own rules quietly, which defeats the purpose for serious users.
What would make this a 5-star app:
an accountability history (unlock usage, schedule adherence, rule changes)
logging Screen Time permission
revocations/restores
• an integrity metric (did I keep my
word or not)
brief, optional reflection prompts at
key moments (before unlocks, after rule changes)
weekly summaries focused on
accountability, not just usage minutes a place to define and revisit why you're limiting apps, so behavior change is internal, not just enforced
Blocking alone changes behavior temporarilv.

reviews.title: Bulk Category Restrictions Needed — Current Process is Too Frustrating
reviews.text:
I really like Clearspace and the features offered in the Pro version, and I appreciate the effort behind the app. However, the inability to apply restrictions to an entire category of apps (like all games) at once is a significant drawback. Having to select and restrict each app individually creates a lot of friction and takes much more time than it should.
This tedious process is actually enough to dissuade me from continuing to use the app, despite its other benefits. Managing multiple apps one by one feels outdated and inefficient, especially when many other apps offer bulk management features.
I understand there may be technical limitations due to Apple’s ScreenTime API, but I strongly urge the Clearspace team to explore solutions for bulk category restrictions or at least a more streamlined multi-app selection process. This improvement would make a huge difference in usability and user retention.
Thanks for listening—I hope to see this feature in future updates!

The screen time is the smaller part of why I like this app though; what I really like is the pushup challenge. I used to do cross country but quit a long time ago, and when i started doing the pushup challenge, it was the first time in about two years i saw an improvement in my body and not a steady decline in my physical condition. I did 1 pushup per 3 minutes for a 31 day challenge, and at the end i noticed it was much easier to do pushups, so I started a 100 day challenge with 1 pushup per 1 minute. I’m a week and a half in and I suddenly realized that over the last month my body has gotten visibly more strong, especially my chest. I can also see my abs more clearly. This little improvement and the fact that I was doing around 50 pushups to 70 pushups a day inspired me, and I finally started working out for the sake of working out again. I lift weights, do pushups, and do core sometimes. It’s not something I spend a huge amount of time on, but im seeing a gradual improvement in my physical condition and willingness to improve my habits. I highly recommend downloading this app.

P.S.
There are a few things wrong with the app; i wish i could put limits on more than one app for free, i uninstalled youtube to keep myself off shorts as an alternative to reels; however, this isnt a huge problem cause there isnt much to do on my phone anyway. 
I also notice that the app has a very hard time realizing if im doing pushups unless im looking straight at the camera and going slow; this hasnt bothered me too much, but sometimes I’ll do like twenty pushups for ten minutes. Usually it works a lil better when im in short sleeves or when i turn on a bunch of lights.
That’s all! Amazing app.

Regardless, I’m going to pay for ClearSpace once the free trial is over. There are small details that make this app more effective (for me, at least) than others like it. For example, ClearSpace you pick how long you want to use the app at a time (from 1-10 minutes) right as you open the app. Then, when time runs out, it says, “the time you set aside for this app is over.” Theoretically I could unlock the app again but I never do…because the app is reminding me that I picked that shorter time (I usually pick 5 minutes, never 10), so I feel compelled to stick to it! I don’t know if that explanation fully makes sense, but trust me, my time spent on social media apps is WAY down since I started using ClearSpace!

I LOVE that if I choose to use one of my locked apps I have pre-determined amounts of use each day and when I use it for the length of time I choose it locks back up again! reviews.title: Suggestions for people who need to use social for work
reviews.text:
This app is perfect for my personal life. I love being able to set up amounts of time allowed on the app, and having to go through a breathing exercise with the mindfulness quote is such a helpful way to be intentional with my time there. I’m likely an outlier in this want, and maybe the paid version offers this (I’m only on the free version). I’m a self employed photographer so naturally I use social media for work related things, such as sourcing talent/models for shoots, responding to inquiries, sending inspo to my marketing team for pre production approval, etc. There are so many times throughout the day I need to go on Instagram to retrieve information for the zoom meeting I’m in or the deck I’m working on. In these moments I want to be fast. A cool option would be “Work Mode” where I don’t have to do a breathing exercise if I’m in a meeting and have people waiting for me to look something up, have the time be 1-2 minutes so I don’t scroll after retrieving work info, and NOT count against the daily opens I’ve allowed myself for personal use. That kind of adds to my internal shame really quickly. I’ve allotted myself 2 opens a day for personal scrolling and want to stick to that for the same million reasons you started this app. But I’ve already opened the app 5 times today strictly for work. And become very impatient/embarrassed when trying to open the app during a meeting. Trust me when I say I think this app is amazing and I want to keep it. If there’s a way to deal with this, I’m here for it.
Editing to add: As someone who is neurodivergent, I can see how a solution to this could also be problematic. If you have an option to use the app without the restraints for work, you can obviously lie and tell ClearSpace it’s for work when you’re just going to mindlessly scroll.
